newsitem.title: JAPAN: Break in weather helps cleanup of Japan oil slick.
newsitem.headline: Break in weather helps cleanup of Japan oil slick.

text.p: A break in bad weather enabled Japanese authorities on Wednesday to launch a full-scale cleanup of oil slicks that have fouled prime fishing areas and coated a 100-km (60-mile) stretch of shoreline.
"The weather has much improved so we can now mount in earnest the cleanup operation," a Maritime Safety Agency spokesman said.

With the wind finally dropping after stormy conditions that had raged since a Russian-registered tanker broke up and started leaking oil on January 2, cleanup work started at first light and was continuing smoothly despite a light snowfall.
The agency deployed 14 ships, two planes and four helicopters to try to find patches of oil drifting towards the shore, drop detergent on it and collect it before more of it reaches land.
Oil has already blackened beaches, threatening economic and environmental disaster for communities which depend on fishing and tourism.
With no real idea of the scale of the problem, maritime authorities said the news was getting worse.
"We are still receiving reports of more places where oil has come ashore," the spokesman added.
At first, authorities estimated that 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) had escaped from the 26-year-old tanker when it broke in half in stormy seas in the Sea of Japan on Thursday.
But they said on Tuesday that the figure appeared too low. The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was carrying a total of 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
Japan's worst oil spill was in 1971 when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil were spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata.

Oil slicks have so far hit shore along a 100 km (60-mile) stretch from Kyoto prefecture in western Japan. The area is dotted with some of Japan's most fertile fishing areas as well as small ports and tourist resorts.
In picturesque Mikuni Bay in Fukui Prefecture, local residents came out in the early morning to gaze forlornly at oil-smeared shores.
Satoshi Horii, 32, an engineer who lives near Mikuni, said it was hard to believe the extent of the damage and he was worried about compensation for the disaster.
"Who's going to pay? The Russians don't have any money so they won't help and yet they are to blame," he told Reuters.

Standing with his five-year-old son, Samu, looking out over the devastated bay, Horii said: "I've been talking to my son about pollution for the last 24 hours. I don't understand and he doesn't understand how it happened and what we can do."
In Mikuni Bay, the oil has surrounded four large flat-topped rocks which were prime spots for growing seaweed, a traditional part of the Japanese diet.
Yukiko Michinoshita, 43, whose husband is a local fisherman, said: "Everything is dead. This was the best part of the coast for abalone and all sorts of fish. They were the sweetest and the best."
A local fisherman's cooperative of about 250 people planned to use homemade scoops made from tin cans to help maritime authorities in the cleanup.
They include women in their seventies whose families have lived in the area for generations.
Cleanup workers were using special chemically treated pads to try to soak up the spill.
Other workers in special protective clothing stood chest-deep in oil-filled waters using hoses to pump out the oil.
